transcript:
[00:00] Priya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — we'll kick off the week 4 sync for the Cobalt pilot. Short agenda: metric review, tuning notes, experiments, then next steps.
[00:12] Alex (Cobalt Eng): Yep, thanks. We've got team members on. Nina and Ethan are here, hi.
[00:20] Jason (Redwood SE): Quick note — I pushed the updated KV cache config yesterday (lowered min-prefix length, enabled session-snapshot mode). The sheet in drive has the raw numbers.
[00:35] Sofia (Cobalt DS): I pulled those, saw the hit rate jump but noticed some variance by route.
[00:42] Priya: Right, global hit moved from ~18% baseline to 46% after the last tuning pass on Friday. That was with relaxed prefix matching and the small token-stitching heuristic.
[00:58] Nina (PM): 46% is promising but for our main chat flow we need closer to 60% to hit the cost targets. Can you break down by route?
[01:10] Jason: Sure — main chat (route: /api/v1/chat) is at 52% hit, knowledge search route is 28%, multi-turn form-fills are 41%. The shared sheet has per-route rows, but I'll paste a filtered view.
[01:27] Alex: The knowledge search low number makes sense — queries are long and less repetitive. We did see a lot of prompt variance because of user metadata injected into early tokens.
[01:38] Priya: That's where prompt normalization comes in — if we canonicalize user metadata into structured placeholders we can improve prefix reuse.
[01:48] Sofia: We tested two approaches offline: full placeholder substitution and loose normalization. Placeholder substitution improved hit on form-flows by +9 percentage points, but changed some outputs slightly.
[01:59] Jason: Important to note — some outputs changed due to removal of explicit user context; we need to surface evals that check quality drift. We'll attach the eval notebooks.
[02:12] Ethan (Security): Quick security question — when you say request logs and raw prompts, what's included? We need PII redaction confirmation and KMS handling.
[02:22] Marissa (CSM): We'll share the SOC2 docs and the audit log architecture; Redwood's log ingestion can be configured to mask tokens at ingestion, and KMS rotates keys. Link shared in chat.
[02:35] Priya: Back to caching — Jason, can you explain session-snapshot/token-stitching? Some of our engineers asked for a plain description.
[02:44] Jason: Yep. Session snapshot is basically capturing the last N tokens of a user session and using that as an extended prefix key in KV cache. Token-stitching tries to map small edits (like punctuation or filler words) to the same cache key so we don't miss hits. It's heuristic-based: we use normalized whitespace, lowercasing, and strip low-information tokens. That bought us a chunk of the improvement.
[03:12] Alex: Any risk of false positives — returning stale cached content when there were user edits that matter?
[03:18] Jason: We guard with TTL and content-change checks. If the model response is sensitive to a particular field removed by normalization, the evals should catch it. Also we have fallback to fresh model generation if a confidence detector flags mismatch.
[03:30] Nina: On TTL experiments — what ranges are we considering?
[03:33] Jason: We proposed 30s, 2m, 5m for initial sweep. Lower TTL favors freshness; higher TTL favors hit-rate. For chat flows with rapid back-and-forth, 30s might be optimal.
[03:45] Sofia: Our offline sim suggested 30s gave best cost/quality tradeoff for high-turn conversations, but for single-turn search 2m was best.
[03:53] Priya: Action — Jason will spin A/B TTL on pilot cluster.
[04:00] Alex: Also curious about eviction policies — LRU vs priority by route. Can we pin keys for long-lived sessions?
[04:06] Jason: Yes, we support pinning at the session level for VIP users; otherwise LRU with per-route quotas. We can try higher per-route quotas for /api/v1/chat.
[04:18] Ethan: On logs again — for the A/B tests, can we limit full logs to a small percentage to reduce exposure?
[04:24] Marissa: Absolutely. We can do 5% full logging and 100% masked metadata.
[04:31] Nina: About quality — we saw a subtle hallucination in the placeholder substitution for two cases last week. Do we have a rollback plan if quality regressions happen?
[04:40] Jason: Yes, rollout via canary with automatic rollback if the eval score drops > 2.5% on the golden prompt set. Canary also runs in parallel with a smaller model fallback.
[04:52] Priya: Nice. Can you also surface the per-token latency change when a cache hit occurs? We need that number for engineering sign-off.
[04:59] Jason: On hits we saw 6-8ms token latency improvement on average for the baseline model; quantized smaller models show larger relative gains. I'll add per-route token-latency columns.
[05:10] Sofia: We also noticed 'burst burn' where cache warming caused brief spikes in token throughput — could be related to the prefetch job.
[05:18] Jason: That's the prefetch worker trying to warm predicted next-prefixes; we can throttle prefetch or add a budget. Prefetch was set aggressive to maximize hits early.
[05:27] Alex: For cost projections if we hit 60% on main chat, what does that look like?
[05:32] Priya: Rough estimate: at 60% hit, token cost for chat route down ~38% on net given our batching and prefix caching assumptions. We'll put concrete numbers in the spreadsheet.
[05:42] Nina: Can you summarise what we need to provide from our side this week?
[05:46] Priya: Sure — provide two canonical prompt templates, mark PII fields; agree to 5% full log sampling for experiments; confirm the load test window.
[05:54] Alex: We'll get those prompt templates by Friday.
[05:58] Jason: Another technical nuance — we found that the KV key namespace was sensitive to tokenization differences across tokenizer versions. Make sure your preprocess pipeline uses the same tokenizer we used in inference.
[06:10] Sofia: Good call — we've pinned tokenizers but will double-check.
[06:14] Marissa: I'll also send the architectural note about private deployment patterns if you consider moving to Redwood Dedicated later.
[06:22] Ethan: If we go Dedicated, does the cache stay in-customer VPC or is it managed? What's the ops boundary?
[06:28] Jason: Dedicated can run the cache in-customer VPC; management plane still coordinates rollouts but data path stays in VPC. We'll send a diagram.
[06:36] Priya: Alright let's run a quick readout of the numbers we agreed on for the agenda: global 46% hit, chat 52%, search 28%, form 41%. Goal chat 60%.
[06:46] Nina: Sounds good. Any blockers?
[06:48] Alex: None beyond getting the prompt templates redacted.
[06:51] Priya: Final recap: Jason TTL A/B, Priya uploads cleaned sheet, Alex shares prompts, Marissa sends SOC2 notes to Ethan, schedule load test for 9/9. We'll reconvene same time next week.
[07:06] Sofia: Quick follow — is there a small experiment we can run to test token-stitching aggressiveness?
[07:12] Jason: Yes — a dial between conservative and aggressive normalization. Conservative strips punctuation only; aggressive removes stopwords like 'um' and personal name tokens. We'll run both across a sampled set.
[07:23] Alex: Please keep quality monitors on. If the aggressive normalization degrades outputs, we'll fallback.
[07:29] Priya: Thanks everyone, end of meeting.
[07:34] [meeting ended]
